title: Rice Ragged Stunt: How to Spot It and Protect Your Palay
metaTitle: Rice Ragged Stunt: Signs, Damage and Control
metaDescription: Rice ragged stunt twists and shreds palay leaves and leaves panicles half out and empty. Learn the signs, the planthopper link and how to protect your crop.
excerpt: Rice ragged stunt is a virus disease that stunts palay and leaves the leaves twisted, serrated and ragged. It has no cure, so you protect the crop by controlling the brown planthopper and by choosing resistant varieties.

heroImage.alt: A brown planthopper on a green leaf. This insect spreads rice ragged stunt from plant to plant
heroImage.credit: portioid, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

blocks.text:
Rice ragged stunt comes from the Rice ragged stunt virus, and the [brown planthopper](/pests/brown-planthopper) carries it from plant to plant. IRRI says the infection is especially high in tropical areas where rice is planted all year round. That gives the insect a field of food at all times.

It often shows up alongside [rice grassy stunt](/diseases/rice-grassy-stunt), because the same insect carries both viruses. IRRI and SEARCA both note that neither disease can be cured. So the plan is to prevent them, starting with the seedbed.

blocks.caption: Quick facts
rows: The whole plant, leaves and panicles and ears
It shows at the early growth stages as stunting, then as leaf twisting and vein swelling at later tillering. It is highest where rice grows all year round.
Brown planthoppers carry the virus. They pick it up within 24 hours of feeding on a sick plant. After about 6 hours they can pass it on, and they stay infective for life.

blocks.text: How to Identify Rice Ragged Stunt

Look at the young crop first. Plants are stunted, with short, dark green leaves that have serrated, uneven edges. The leaf tip or base may twist into a spiral, and the ragged parts turn yellow to yellow brown. At later tillering, pale to dark brown swellings, called galls, run along the veins on the outside of the leaf blade and the sheath. At heading, the panicle comes out only in part and carries unfilled grains.

items: Plants are severely stunted in the early growth stages, with short, dark green leaves.
Leaf edges are serrated and uneven, and the ragged parts turn yellow to yellow brown.
Leaf blades twist at the tip or the base into a spiral.
Swollen veins, pale yellow, white or dark brown, appear on the leaf blades and the sheaths.
Flowering is late, panicles come out in part, and many grains stay unfilled.

blocks.title: Do not confuse it with
blocks.text: Plants hit by ragged stunt are often confused with [rice tungro](/diseases/rice-tungro) or grassy stunt, since all of them stunt the crop. Ragged stunt has the torn, serrated leaf edges and the swollen veins. Grassy stunt has the grassy clump with rusty spots, and tungro gives an orange yellow color.
How Rice Ragged Stunt Hurts Your Palay

IRRI says rice ragged stunt cuts yield by causing panicles that come out only in part, unfilled grains and a loss of plant density. A sick plant can survive, but its yield falls sharply. We found no sourced yield loss percentage for the Philippines, so we give none.

The damage grows with the number of planthoppers. Young nymphs spread the virus most efficiently, so the seedbed and the first weeks matter most. The planthopper itself also burns whole patches of rice, a damage called hopperburn. In 2017, SEARCA reported a resurgence of the insect across 18 provinces, with the two viruses it carries having no cure.
How to Control Rice Ragged Stunt

items: Choose a resistant variety. The Lucid rice key says resistant varieties are probably the most important control. Three kinds exist: resistant to the planthopper, resistant to the virus, and resistant to both.
Plant at the same time as the farms around you, so the planthoppers do not move from older fields to young ones.
Scout the seedbed and the young crop every week for planthoppers at the base of the plants.
Protect the spiders, mirid bugs and egg parasite wasps that eat planthoppers, by avoiding early insecticide sprays.
Pull out and bury sick plants early, and destroy infected stubble and crop residue after harvest.
Flood the seedbed for a day when planthoppers are on it, so that the insects drown.

blocks.text: No spray cures a plant that has the virus, because infected plants cannot recover. A spray can only target the planthopper. IRRI and PhilRice advise against insecticide in the first 30 to 40 days after transplanting unless a pest is truly at outbreak level. Early sprays kill the spiders and wasps and then cause planthopper outbreaks. If an outbreak is real, ask your local agriculture office which FPA registered product suits your field, and follow the label.

blocks.title: Spray safely
blocks.text: Use only products registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label for the rate, the timing and the protective clothing. Switch to a different fungicide group next time, so the disease does not learn to survive it. Our [guide to plant diseases](/diseases/plant-diseases-philippines) explains how.

items: Plant resistant varieties, and plant together with your neighbors.
Break the cycle by leaving the field fallow or rotating when you can, so volunteer rice does not keep the virus.
Scout the seedbed and the crop every week through tillering.
Hold off on early insecticide sprays, so the natural enemies can work.
Keep records of which lots had stunted patches, and plant them first with a resistant variety.

blocks.text: Not Sure What You Are Seeing?

Take a clear photo of the spots or the damage up close, then the whole plant, then ask [Anee, the smart farm technician](/features/ai-agricultural-technician) in anee.io, in Tagalog or English. blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Rice Ragged Stunt

items.q: Can rice ragged stunt be cured?
items.a: No. IRRI says infected plants cannot recover. The way to protect your crop is to control the brown planthopper and plant resistant varieties.

items.q: Is ragged stunt the same as grassy stunt?
items.a: No. They are two different viruses, but the same brown planthopper carries both, and they can appear in the same field.
The virus causes galls, or swellings, along the veins on the outside of the leaf blades and sheaths. They are one of the clearest signs of ragged stunt.
